blocks.md: This lesson follows **From a Useful Proposal to an Accepted Task** in *Introduction* (Vol III).

blocks.source: Vol III, Introduction, § From a Useful Proposal to an Accepted Task
blocks.md: That gap between a model response and a finished job is concrete when an engineering team delegates a repository repair: diagnosing and fixing an intermittent race condition in a distributed key-value store. A foundation model can inspect the issue description and propose an edit to the connection-pool locking logic. Emitting that patch text, however, leaves the repository untouched.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Cost per accepted task matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Under retry-until-accept, C_eff = E[C_attempt]/p_acc, so acceptance divides the whole attempt cost and any mechanism pays for its overhead only if it lowers this ratio.

questions.q: The section **From a Useful Proposal to an Accepted Task** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Self-report, static analysis, visible tests, sealed tests, and formal verification form a default ordering of acceptance evidence that coverage can override, and every check is a bounded claim narrower than the task.
The characteristic agent failure is well-formed, credible, and wrong, so fail-stop monitors record success and agreement among samples from one model sets no bound on wrong answers.

The ordered record of states, proposals, runtime decisions, and observations from initial context to acceptance, termination, or escalation is the accounting boundary for cost, latency, state lifetime, quotas, and permissions, so resources are managed per task rather than per call.
Under retry-until-accept, C_eff = E[C_attempt]/p_acc, so acceptance divides the whole attempt cost and any mechanism pays for its overhead only if it lowers this ratio.
